questions.question: What is the primary practical motivation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) when adapting very large pretrained models to many downstream tasks?
questions.choice_A: Reducing the storage and distribution cost by keeping the core model frozen and shipping only small task-specific parameters
questions.choice_B: Significantly increasing inference speed by pruning most layers
questions.choice_C: Increasing model capacity by adding more layers during fine-tuning
questions.choice_D: Improving the quality of pretraining without collecting more data

questions.question: In classic adapter-based fine-tuning for Transformers, which parameters are typically updated during training?
questions.choice_A: All attention and feed-forward layers in the base model
questions.choice_B: Only the newly inserted adapter modules while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen
questions.choice_C: Only the layer normalization parameters throughout the network
questions.choice_D: Only the embedding matrix and the final classification head

questions.question: How does prefix tuning differ from prompt tuning in Transformer models?
questions.choice_A: Prefix tuning modifies only the embedding matrix, while prompt tuning modifies attention key/value states
questions.choice_B: Prefix tuning inserts trainable modules inside each residual block, while prompt tuning freezes all layers
questions.choice_C: Prefix tuning optimizes virtual key/value vectors prepended to each layer’s attention, while prompt tuning learns trainable input tokens at the embedding layer only
questions.choice_D: Prefix tuning and prompt tuning are the same method with different names

questions.question: Which statement best describes LoRA’s parameterization for adapting a weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$?
questions.choice_A: LoRA replaces $W$ by a smaller matrix and upsamples it during inference
questions.choice_B: LoRA trains a low-rank $W$ from scratch and discards the pretrained $W$
questions.choice_C: LoRA factorizes $W$ as $W = U\Sigma V^\top$ and trains only $\Sigma$
questions.choice_D: LoRA keeps $W$ frozen and learns a low-rank update $\Delta W = B A$ of rank $r \ll \min(m,n)$, so the effective weight is $W + \Delta W$

questions.question: What is a common effect of using LoRA on training-time memory and compute compared to full fine-tuning?
questions.choice_A: Lower gradient memory and optimizer state because only the low-rank factors are trainable, with similar forward-pass cost
questions.choice_B: Higher forward-pass compute due to repeated SVD computations
questions.choice_C: Much higher activation memory because LoRA duplicates all layers
questions.choice_D: No change in memory or compute footprint relative to full fine-tuning

questions.question: How does the rank $r$ in LoRA typically affect adaptation quality and resource usage?
questions.choice_A: Higher $r$ usually reduces capacity and increases storage sublinearly
questions.choice_B: Higher $r$ usually increases capacity and storage roughly linearly, with modest inference overhead
questions.choice_C: Lower $r$ yields strictly better performance due to stronger regularization
questions.choice_D: The choice of $r$ only affects training stability, not final performance

questions.question: What initialization strategy is commonly used for LoRA to preserve the pretrained model’s function at the start of fine-tuning?
questions.choice_A: Initialize both low-rank factors with large random values to escape flat minima
questions.choice_B: Initialize with an SVD of the pretrained weights to match $\Delta W$ to $W$
questions.choice_C: Initialize so that $\Delta W = 0$ (e.g., one factor near-zero and the other random), making the initial effective weight equal to the frozen $W$
questions.choice_D: Initialize by copying the full pretrained weight into the low-rank factors

questions.question: Compared to additive updates, what property is most characteristic of multiplicative weight updates when adapting pretrained networks?
questions.choice_A: They always reduce the Lipschitz constant of the network
questions.choice_B: They guarantee orthogonality of updated features
questions.choice_C: They are equivalent to adding a low-rank matrix to each weight
questions.choice_D: They modulate existing weights proportionally to their magnitude, making adaptations scale-sensitive

questions.question: In Pivotal Tuning Inversion (PTI) for diffusion models, what is the role of the "pivotal" representation?
questions.choice_A: It is an optimized subject-specific embedding or latent that anchors subsequent, limited weight updates to preserve identity while improving fidelity
questions.choice_B: It is a randomly sampled noise seed that stabilizes training
questions.choice_C: It is a separate encoder network trained from scratch to generate prompts
questions.choice_D: It is a regularization term that penalizes large gradients

questions.question: Which of the following best characterizes DreamBooth-style adaptation for image generation?
questions.choice_A: Training only the text encoder on millions of images from the target class
questions.choice_B: Fine-tuning with a small set of subject images and a class-specific prior preservation loss to retain generality while capturing the subject
questions.choice_C: Replacing the UNet with a low-rank factorization learned from scratch
questions.choice_D: Freezing the entire model and optimizing only classifier-free guidance weights

questions.question: Where are adapter modules typically inserted in Transformer architectures?
questions.choice_A: Only before the embedding layer
questions.choice_B: After the final layer norm at the end of the model
questions.choice_C: Within each residual block, often between the sublayer output and the residual connection, using a down-projection, nonlinearity, and up-projection
questions.choice_D: Inside the softmax of the attention mechanism

questions.question: Which statement about the relative expressivity of prompt tuning versus adapters is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Prompt tuning is strictly more expressive because it modifies every layer’s hidden states
questions.choice_B: Adapters are strictly less expressive because they add a bottleneck
questions.choice_C: Both are equally expressive for any fixed parameter budget
questions.choice_D: Prompt tuning often has lower capacity because it only affects the model via input embeddings, whereas adapters can modify intermediate representations

questions.question: What is a key advantage of distributing task-specific adapters or LoRA weights instead of full fine-tuned models?
questions.choice_A: They are small and can be composed with a shared base model, reducing storage, bandwidth, and licensing/IP concerns
questions.choice_B: They universally improve inference latency, regardless of hardware
questions.choice_C: They eliminate the need for the original pretrained model
questions.choice_D: They remove the risk of overfitting on small datasets

questions.question: How can multiple LoRA adapters for different skills be combined at inference time on the same base model, assuming architectural compatibility?
questions.choice_A: They cannot be combined; only one LoRA can be active
questions.choice_B: By linearly summing their low-rank updates $\Delta W$ with task-specific scaling coefficients, optionally gating per layer
questions.choice_C: By multiplying their low-rank factors to create a higher-rank factorization
questions.choice_D: By replacing the base weight $W$ with the largest-magnitude update among them

questions.question: For adapting diffusion models with PEFT, which layers are most commonly targeted by LoRA to balance quality and cost?
questions.choice_A: Only the output convolution layers
questions.choice_B: Only the text encoder embeddings
questions.choice_C: Attention modules (self- and cross-attention) within the UNet, sometimes with selected MLPs
questions.choice_D: All layers uniformly, including normalization and positional encodings

questions.question: Why can parameter-efficient strategies help mitigate overfitting and catastrophic forgetting compared to full-model fine-tuning on small datasets?
questions.choice_A: They freeze dropout, which improves generalization
questions.choice_B: They increase the number of trainable parameters but reduce the learning rate
questions.choice_C: They replace the loss function with a contrastive objective
questions.choice_D: They constrain the optimization to a smaller subspace (e.g., adapters or low-rank updates), preserving more of the pretrained capabilities

questions.question: Which technique typically increases inference-time compute the most due to its mechanism of prepending additional vectors to attention across layers?
questions.choice_A: Prefix tuning
questions.choice_B: LoRA
questions.choice_C: Adapter modules
questions.choice_D: Bitfit (bias-only fine-tuning)

questions.question: Which statement about the identifiability of LoRA’s low-rank factors is correct?
questions.choice_A: The factorization is unique for any given $\Delta W$
questions.choice_B: The factorization is non-unique; for invertible $R$, $BA = (BR)(R^{-1}A)$ represents the same $\Delta W$
questions.choice_C: Identifiability is guaranteed by initializing $A$ to zero
questions.choice_D: Identifiability requires $r = \min(m,n)$

questions.question: From an optimization perspective, why might LoRA sometimes converge faster or more stably than full fine-tuning?
questions.choice_A: Because it eliminates the need for backpropagation
questions.choice_B: Because it increases the number of free parameters beyond the base model
questions.choice_C: Because it constrains updates to a low-dimensional subspace, which can improve conditioning and reduce the risk of overfitting
questions.choice_D: Because it replaces the loss with a convex objective

questions.question: When comparing additive and multiplicative adaptation mechanisms, in which scenario are multiplicative updates particularly desirable?
questions.choice_A: When the goal is to introduce entirely new features orthogonal to existing ones
questions.choice_B: When one needs to sparsify the model by zeroing out weights
questions.choice_C: When low-rank approximation error must be minimized
questions.choice_D: When the goal is to modulate feature amplitudes (e.g., via learned scales) without changing the underlying feature subspace

questions.question: Which statement about the trade-offs between PEFT methods and full fine-tuning is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: PEFT methods always match or exceed full fine-tuning performance on every task
questions.choice_B: PEFT methods cannot overfit because they train few parameters
questions.choice_C: PEFT methods often achieve competitive performance with far fewer trainable parameters, but may underperform on tasks requiring large, global representational changes
questions.choice_D: PEFT methods require training-time access to the full pretraining corpus
